$doc: Host-authoritative WebRTC P2P. The signalling server (src/server) only brokers 6-digit codes and SDP/ICE; all gameplay traffic is peer-to-peer. See docs/systems/NETWORKING.md.

signalling.$note: The socket to the signalling server is not the peer links: losing it costs nobody their game, but it stops anyone else joining and never comes back on its own. So it is re-opened on this backoff, quietly, while play carries on.

identity.$doc: A player's name is the only free text in the protocol other than chat, so its cap lives here rather than with the interface that draws it: it is applied to what this player types AND to whatever a peer sends.

simulation.$doc: The simulation runs on a fixed tick that is deliberately independent of the display: a 30 fps machine takes two steps a frame and a 240 Hz one takes none most frames, and both reach the same world state after the same second of real time.
simulation.$note: A frame that arrives late is caught up, up to this much real time in one go. Beyond it the debt is dropped rather than paid, because a machine that cannot keep up will only fall further behind trying - the alternative is a spiral where every frame owes more than the last.
simulation.$note2: requestAnimationFrame stops in a window that is not in front, and the host simulates the run for everybody. When no frame has arrived for this long the loop is pumped from a timer instead, so a host who alt-tabs does not stop the world.

interpolation.$doc: Remote bodies are drawn from a buffer that plays back in the past, so there is always a sample on each side of the playback head. The delay ADAPTS: it is the smallest buffer that still covers what this connection is actually doing, measured continuously, so a good link stays responsive and a choppy one stops stuttering.
interpolation.$note: How many multiples of the measured arrival jitter the buffer holds on top of `baseDelayMs`. Two covers the great majority of arrivals on a normal connection.
interpolation.$note2: Growing the buffer is urgent (a body has already stuttered); shrinking it is not, and doing it quickly would make the delay itself a source of jitter. So they have very different time constants.
interpolation.$note3: Transit times are measured against a clock offset estimated from the fastest packet seen in this window. A window keeps it honest as the two machines' clocks drift apart.

channels.$doc: Two data channels over ONE peer connection. The `state` channel is negotiated out of band on a fixed id, which is what lets it be created without a second ICE negotiation.

state.$note: Unordered and never retransmitted. A snapshot that has to wait for an older one to be re-sent is worse than one that never arrives - the next is already on its way. This is the single biggest thing between choppy wifi and a body that jumps.

connection.$doc: Liveness, recovery and the load gate. A browser tab closed without a goodbye never sends one, so peers are judged on silence rather than on a close event - but silence on a bad connection is not the same thing as a peer that has gone.
connection.$note: Three stages, not two. Past `unstableSeconds` the link is reported as struggling and recovery starts; only past `timeoutSeconds` is the peer actually gone. Dropping somebody for a ten-second wifi hiccup is the failure this gap exists to prevent.
connection.$note2: A link that CLOSES is a peer that has gone, and is dropped at once rather than waited out - the timeout above is for silence, which is a different thing.
connection.$note3: Round-trip time is measured off the heartbeat and smoothed over this many samples. It is what the connection indicator reports.
connection.$note4: Everyone generates the map at their own speed. The host holds the run at the loading screen until every peer reports in, or until this expires - a peer that crashed loading must not strand the rest at a spinner.

hostMigration.$note: Not implemented in v1. If the host drops, the run ends and everyone returns to the main menu.

voice.$doc: Proximity voice over the same peer connections. Attenuation is computed client-side per remote peer.
voice.$note: Attenuation is distance only. Walls and doors do not muffle voice - players are meant to hear each other generously across the map.
voice.$note2: The enemy only gets a noise event above `noiseThresholdDb` - well above the open-mic gate, so a whisper carries to your team and not to the hunter. Speaking re-emits every `noiseIntervalSeconds`; noise events live one tick.
voice.$note3: Speaking indicators: what counts as audible on a received track, and how long the icon lingers so it does not flicker between words.

steam.$doc: Placeholder for the packaged build. Not used in the browser build.
